segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What is your English name?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: They call me Charlie Dewey Keener.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about Cherokee?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Same Charlie Dewey Keener.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Keener.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah, Keener. That’s what it says on the paper my mom said. It’s Dewey Keener.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Dewey Keener. Where was you born?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Towards Lost City—Fourteen Mile Creek. There’s a lot of us that live there, near Lost City Fourteen Mile Creek. There’s a lot of Cherokees live there. By the creek up on top.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was you born in a hospital?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah. About ten in the family. We lived up on top, by the road.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that where you grew up, around Lost City?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah. Fourteen Mile Creek. But, now, there’s a lot of us live there—Cherokees. About ten families. We’re all cousins. There’s a lot of us boys and girls running around the creek. We’d be chasing crawdads and fish. And we’d go to the creek, swimming.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you lived there ever since you born?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah. At first, let’s see. We lived there when I was a baby. And, fifth through sixth school [grade], we got on a bus. We knew Cherokee. We all got back on the bus, and we went to Wyandotte school. But, when we got there, all the other kids were crying. Crying for their mom and dad. I stayed from first grade through fifth at Wyandotte. Everybody else went back towards Lost City. But I stayed. I liked it ’cause they was giving me clothes and shoes. And I was taking a bath and shower. That’s what I liked about it. When we first got there all we talked was Cherokee. When the teacher said something, I didn’t believe it. And, when I was sitting in school, they told me to write my name—but I didn’t understand it. There was a girl, sitting in front, she wrote her name. And [so], I wrote her name [too]. They said, “That’s not your name. Is that your name?” I told them, “Yeah.” But I didn’t understand it. He was saying I was lying. “You’re not a girl—that’s a girl’s name that you wrote.” And we got spanked for speaking. All the time they told me not to be speaking Cherokee. I understand a little bit of what they were saying. They told me not to be speaking Cherokee. I told them, “That’s all I know.” And then when it was recess, then I couldn’t go ’cause of that—I spoke Cherokee. Then I went out for a long time. Then I started understanding what the White people were saying. Then it was OK.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you was forbidden to talk Cherokee?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah, sometimes I would cry. But I was by myself, and sometimes I would cry. I guess the White people was doing good. I thought, “I guess it’s like that everywhere.” But, myself, I really didn’t know what they done, outside, you know... That’s what I thought. But, [after] six months, I guess, something like that, I understood what the White people were saying. Then I started doing good. That one time. Let’s see... about fourth or fifth [grade] I think, I was with some boys that were my friends, and we were there [at school]. They said, “Let’s go to the house.” And I thought, “OK.” And I said, “OK.” And I went with both of them. We went by the store. “We’re going to the house.” “Where are you going?” I didn’t know where I was at. I didn’t know which way home was. They took off. I stood around and then I went back towards the school. Now I was scared. I didn’t know where I was at. All I knew was the school. Then I went to where I lived, a dormitory. I stayed there for fifth and sixth grade and I played basketball. That’s it, basketball. Yeah, fifth and sixth. I went through the dormitory—them boys were big. We were in there. Me and two boys stayed in a room. We were cleaning the room ’cause there was an inspection every Saturday. If you did good you got a pass to go on the hill, if you wanted to go. Or, in town Wyandotte, you could go. That’s what we did. But I’ve been there a long time. I liked getting clothes and water, and to take a good shower. But still I went to Wyandotte. About sixth grade my grandma passed away. So I had to go back to Lost City. I went to school. When I finished Lost City, I went to Hulbert. I finished 12th grade at Hulbert. When I finished at Hulbert, I really liked football. And then I went to Lawrence, Kansas Junior College football. I went to school in Lawrence, Kansas for a little while. Then I quit and came back to Hulbert.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Then, I just worked everywhere. Labor—hauled hay, just different things to make money. And then I joined the Labor Union. I worked all over Tulsa. Then I quit that, and I was reading the paper, and I seen they was needing a railroad worker. I went, got an application. I got on [the railroad] for about two years. Railroad work was hard work. You had to work in the winter and when it was raining. No rain out, no snow, no nothing. We was in the truck and, “How come the others have bags?” I thought, “Why do they have bags?” When it rained, I knew—they had raincoats on. I didn’t have a raincoat. I was standing around wet. I was walking around like a duck. But I liked that, I worked for about a year in the railroad.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: And I thought, “That was hard.” And my cousin worked all over, like—Tulsa, New York, Kansas City—he worked all over. He was an iron worker. That’s what he wanted to do. I told [him], “I think I’m scared to go all over the place, I’ve never been anywhere.” I told him, “Yeah, I’ll go with you.” We went all over the United States. But the radio tower, yeah, the radio tower and telephone tower—we was building those. It was real high—680 feet. We was making good money. I stayed with them ’till I retired.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: My wife stayed home with my son and one daughter “Why don’t you ever go to the store?” -- “I have to work [if] you want clothes and babies, too,” [I said]. I stayed with them ’long time. ’Till I retired [from iron work], that’s what I did.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: And, where I was born, I was born at Hastings Hospital [Cherokee Nation W. W. Hastings Hospital, Tahlequah, Oklahoma]. That very first one, I was born there. And then we went back towards Hulbert and Lost City. Yeah, we went to the creek a lot of times. Above where the branch went through. We was always there looking for crawdads—get an old tire, and get it muddy. We there, naked. They would say, “There’s a car coming.” We would go up the hill. We was at Fourteen Mile Creek and Lost City. I went to school at Lost City—sixth, seventh grade. And then I went to Hulbert. We was walking to school. We walked four miles—that’s pretty far. We had a road above. And there were 5 of us, we was walking like ducks on top. And, the teacher had a car at her house, and we would get in there. We would get in [and go] towards Lost City. It was good to ride in a car. We was just walking around.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You played football before?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah, at Hulbert. I used to like it. We played [teams] Little Kansas, Colcord... Let’s see... Yeah, basketball—Lost City, we played basketball at Lost City. We was really good, [in] seventh and eighth grade. And we played Sequoyah [team], that’s it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: My family?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Four. My dad, my mom, one brother, and one sister. Me and... We would gather at the creek above. My brother went to Chilocco to go to school. I didn’t hardly see him when I went to school, at Hulbert and Lost City. I didn’t hardly see him when he went to Chilocco. I didn’t see him anymore. Sometimes he comes back to the house. He stays for just for a little while, then he leaves again. But I don’t know which way he goes, I don’t ask him. And, my sister, she’s by herself. We’re by ourselves. It’s the same—she lives in Lost City, and she finished in Hulbert. And, when I went to back to Hulbert, I graduated Lost City—I mean Hulbert—and then I worked everywhere. I came home every once in a while. I was making good money. I was chasing money. I bought myself a automobile—a new one. Boy, I felt good driving a automobile. And clothes were good. I liked working. Sometimes, when I went home, I gave my mom money. And, my dad, he would ask, “You making pretty good money?” And I would tell him, “Yeah, that’s why I give y’all money. It might help y’all out a little bit.” They liked it good. What I’m saying—where we was born, at Fourteen Mile Creek, where we lived at was a log house. Where we lived—two room log house. It was small, and it didn’t have electricity and running water, that’s where we lived.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Them towers you said y’all built, was you climbing them?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Huh?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Them towers you said y’all were fixing?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Uh-huh!

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was you climbing around?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah, all the time. That broken-express-that’s-high. You can see the left-hand side—that’s where I got on. I helped them. That’s where I worked, for about six months. I went everywhere doing that, and then New York, and Kansas City, California, Texas, Mississippi, and Georgia. I didn’t like New York—there was too many people. If you see someone, they don’t do anything, they just walk off. Like Texas, Louisiana—they’ll talk good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You’ve been everywhere?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Uh. Yeah, everywhere. Let’s see, I think it was New York. A Mohawk called after me, “Are you Mohawk?” he said. “I’m Cherokee,” I told him. “Where are you from?” --I told him, “Oklahoma.” -- “Do you still stay in a teepee?” I said, “No.” Every time I go north—New York and Minnesota, back in there, they think Cherokees still live in teepees. I tell them, “No, they don’t.” But—down towards Texas and Louisiana—they don’t do that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did all of y’all talk Cherokee?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Uh yeah, my dad, my mom, we all talked Cherokee. Like what I was telling you at first, time [was] they wasn’t allowing us to talk [Cherokee]. I understood English a little bit. When we got on the bus we went to Seneca, I can still understand English a little bit. Sometimes, everybody that was in there would talk Cherokee. All of them were my cousins, and we would all talk Cherokee. What I was saying, when I was told to write my name—I understood a little bit, what I was being told. When the girl wrote her name—I wrote her name [too]. “[But] that’s not your name.” “What? Did you hear?” I didn’t understand it what that-one said. I understood a little bit, but “Why did you do that?” that-one said. “I don’t,” I told that-One. That-one said, “Why are you standing around your desk? Don’t be standing around.” That-one said, “You’re lying to me.” I didn’t really understand that-One when they told me I was lying. I laughed a little. I didn’t know what that-One was saying. Boy, the teacher got really mad. That-one told me to come here. I followed that-one. I was standing at the corner. I was told just to stand there, and that-one told me, “No recess.” I thought, “I wonder why that-one done that?” Recess, I wasn’t going to recess. Then the bell ring, they all went out. I was going to follow them. The teacher said, “Hey! You stay here. You lied to me about speaking Cherokee. You was standing around.” It’s all woods now. A while back, when we lived on the hill, when I was still going to school, Sears Romade... I think it was Sears Roebuck—they were selling them everywhere. A White person... My dad, my dad was working. My mom said, “A White person is coming, they’re running” Boy, [unintelligible] Then we went up on the hill—we were hiding. “How come you’re sitting up on the hill?” “I’m scared of the White people.” I’ve been afraid of White people since I was a little kid. That’s why I go up the hill.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: And then my mom always used to tell me about the little people. Whenever we got through eating, and, like bread. And she went outside, and went up the hill, I asked her, “Where you going?” “I’m going to feed the little men.” “What is it?” I didn’t understand it—little? There ain’t any living [here], y’all are the only ones living here. “There’s some little people living on top of the hill,” that’s what my mom always told me. And then, when I went down to the creek, they’re laughing and talking—the little ones live by the creek. I always sit there, but I never seen them. And, when I go outside, I go hunting—just for squirrels. I went up on the hill. They told me I could see the little people. I wanted to see them, but that didn’t happen. That’s the only thing my mom told me—was that there was some little people living. And, still, right now, the Cherokees will tell you there are little people living. How ’bout you—you think they’re living? Do you see them?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Who were your parents? What were their names?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: My mom... I don’t know nothing about my dad. Her dad [my maternal grandad] ain’t alive. Nancy Wells and John Wells. It’s them Wells, and them Smiths, that’s all I know. My dad was John Wells.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were they from around Lost City? Did they come from there?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah, there—Lost City. Like I was saying, they all live there—Lost City, Fourteen Mile Creek.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about the stuff to get by with? Was it coming to y’all easy, or was y’all hitting it kinda hard?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Uh yeah, that one. Maybe about four miles, maybe, we all lived there. And people... And, on Memorial Day, my mom only made pies. She made a lot of them. And new, five or six years old, they bought [us] new pants and shirts. And on decoration we were at Keener Church. There was a lot of us there, they were eating in a big church and clean dining room and ... They weren’t that much high [price of]. Pretty clothes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all use to have garden?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What all did y’all plant?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: You mean outside?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Just anything—like onion, let’s see... Radish, ‘cumbers, and corn. “When you go in the garden don’t eat anything. Or if you’re eating bread, don’t eat it in the garden.” I asked, “How come?” They told me, “The corn won’t make it.” I was told, “If you’re hungry, eat in the house, don’t eat in the garden.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I was told the same thing.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: We had pigs—one or two. We ate pig. My dad would put [a pig] in the smokehouse in the wintertime. That pig would hang there, in the winter, and we would eat it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And when we had been to a funeral, we was told not to go in the garden. We was told not to go in.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: One time we had a cow. And when we got done the garden, the cow would be in there, eating what it thought belonged to it. It ate it. We had chickens. We had a lot of chickens. We was eating eggs. And, them pigs, sometimes by the light and then the pigs would stay on the hill. And, the evening, they all come back down to the house. And, then, they would leave again. But, at nighttime, they would stay by the house all the time, ’cause they want to eat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What do you remember about what your mom cooked? What did you like best about what she cooked?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: All the time... Well really... All we ate was potatoes, beans, and cornbread, really. We ate kanuchi all the time. But, now, there’s not really any Cherokees eating kanuchi. ’Long time ago that’s all we ate—kanuchi. But now there’s hardly any Cherokees eating kanuchi. If you buy it—it’s $5 a ball! But, like what I’m saying, ’long time ago all Cherokees ate kanuchi, but now they’re hardly eating it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I make kanuchi.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I make it. Right now, I have eight to make.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They’ve asked for them.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Really? Where I come from, they don’t make that anymore. That’s what I’m saying. If they find it, they buy it—kanuchi—$5 a ball. What I was saying, really, I think there ain’t that many Cherokees making kanuchi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s hard to find nuts right now.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: How about, that one time, the same thing I’m doing—talking. They say, “Are you prejudice?” I told them, “Yeah.” “Why?” ’Cause, when I was a baby, we lived in a White neighborhood. When I was in school, I got paddling for talking Cherokee. And, when I went to a house White people lived, I was scared of White people. “Why?” “I don’t know.” They told me, “They will take you away.” I just went up the hill. They told me, “You’re not suppose to do that. You live here,” they told me, “The White people really didn’t like the Cherokees. And when you get married, don’t get a White person. Get a Cherokee woman, so you can have a good family.” That’s what my mom told me. That’s what I was always told, “Don’t be chasing White girls. Just chase Cherokees.” “Why?” “’Cause right now we’re talking Cherokee, and, in about 10-15 years really, the Cherokees ain’t going to be talking it” that’s what my mom told me. That’s how it is right now—hardly any Cherokee talking. Right now, if you’re with someone you love, we ask them, “You talk Cherokee? And when you talk English, don’t forget how to speak Cherokee.” To me, I think that’s what’s really happening.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about you, already mentioned it a little bit --

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: ...Huh?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: ...you mentioned ‘while ago, where you grew up. What was it like where you grew up at?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah. Really, I don’t understand what you are saying.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where you grew up at, at your house, how was it? What was it like, was it wooded area?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah, it was all woods—like I told you ’while ago. It was like at the creek, it was on the hill, it was all Cherokee. There was no White people around. You couldn’t see them. There wasn’t any White people living there. All of us Cherokees lived there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all help each other out?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah, we all helped each other out. If somebody needed something, they [the other locals] would go there and work. And if they wanted something, they would give it to them. Or if they needed wood, they would cut wood. [For the] wood stove... Cook stove. If someone was sick, they would go there and cut wood.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: All of y’all that was [living] close—were all of y’all family?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Me, I like that. But, now, nobody won’t help out, if you need anything. To me that was good—up the hill, Fourteen Mile Creek and Lost City. If you live there, someone can help you. Right now, if we were in town, nobody would help you.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They used to call it everyone, gadugi—when everybody helped each other out.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Right now, some of the real Cherokees, when the elders want something, nobody helps them. And when somebody runs for chief, whatever, “I’m going to help the elders.” I know two or three that really wants something—like houses. But nobody is there. Me, I don’t know but if someone goes there... But if someone goes there, they say something to the White person. If a Cherokee wants something they call them White people. Them Cherokee say, “I don’t understand, you need to go here...” Where’s that at? Tahlequah. I wrote down the telephone, they wouldn’t do it. “How come you won’t go [to Tahlequah]? They will help you if you go.” I don’t know. I really didn’t understand what they were saying. Really, they were speaking English. But if you’re talking Cherokee. Like if you talk, or if he talks, Cherokee. When you talk Cherokee, you would tell him, “What you talking about?” in Cherokee, and [they] can help me. I feel sorry for them right now, the Cherokees, I think.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In about 20 years, what do you think about how the Cherokees are going to be living like?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: I really don’t know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you think it’s going to be harder for them?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. It’s like what I’m saying—when I said they will help the Cherokees that don’t speak hardly English—Cherokee is all they know. Somebody that lives in Tahlequah, Jay, or Salina [in Oklahoma], someone that knows Cherokee. Nobody goes there didn’t speak Cherokee. But the real Cherokee... I didn’t understand it [what happened]: Then they gave the old lady some papers, and told her, “You have to do this—write your name, how many are in the house. When you finish, come here. I will help you with the paperwork,” they don’t understand. She says, “I don’t understand.” Sometimes, that one time, on paper, that-One wrote their name. And [kept it] for about a month, then she threw it away, “Nobody will help me.” I asked that-One, “How come they won’t help you?” That-One said, “If I was a White person, or if I was half-White they would help me. I’m full blood Cherokee—they won’t help me. They’ll help you if you [can] tell someone what you want them to do. Yeah, really if you tell someone, they might help you. But I didn’t understand how to write or read it somewhere. Then nobody came for about a month, so I just threw the papers away.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How about the Cherokee language? In about 20 years how do you think it’s going to be like to speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Like I was saying, at first there’s going to be a few that will speak Cherokee. They’re not hardly speaking English. Like here, what y’all are saying—the little ones, they want to speak Cherokee. That’s real good. But when they quit school, and when they get back home, they are going to forget it. But if there’s a Cherokee in the home, if they speak it all the time. Like what I’m saying [is] they’re doing good talking Cherokee. But when they go home, they are going to forget it, at home. That’s how it’s going to be. That’s what’s happening right now. You have to talk Cherokee all the time. I forget to say something too, sometimes. But I bought a Cherokee book, so I look it up. It’s like what I’m saying, we have to talk Cherokee all the time—or you’re going to forget it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you believe that the Cherokee language is going to end?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Huh?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you believe that the Cherokee language is going to end?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Ah, I don’t know. How about, that one time, my granddaughter went to school at Sequoyah. When she finished, she got that Gates Scholarship and OU. And she went to OSU, but she’s working at Northeastern. She’s making good money. She said “I really don’t understand what they’re doing, speaking Cherokee. I want to learn how to write Cherokee, and I want to learn how to talk it. Like if I have to fill out an application, or something,” to learn, I guess. And I said, “Is that what you really want to do?” She said, “Yeah.” I said, “That’s real good, if you want to do that.” I told her, “If you really want to do that, go for it.”

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: But she’s making good money at Northeastern... But she wants to talk Cherokee, and she wants to write it. And I can’t sign it and fill it out, she has an interview sometime this month. Next week sometime. I really don’t know. And she’s going to school—she’s been going to school for two years. She can talk a little bit of Cherokee. What you learned from home, what we talk—that’s good. I told her, “That’s what I want you to do.” We’re always talking Cherokee. Like I was saying earlier, if you don’t talk Cherokee you’ll forget it. That’s what she wants to do. I told her that’s good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you have grandkids?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Huh?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you have grandkids? Grandkids?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah, she’s the oldest grandkid. And, the other one, she works at Hastings, she a nurse. And my grandson, that’s who I was helping. He was at my house. He went to school at North Dakota and South Dakota to be a doctor. When he finished school, he went to North Dakota—at the Reservation up there—to go to work. And then South Dakota. And then Oklahoma City—they took him to the cancer deal, or something. But I don’t think he liked that. When he finished that, he became an ER doctor here at Hastings. He works at night 7-7.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: In 20 years, what do you think they will have to work on? What kind of work do you think they will have then?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: I think real good—if they all go to school. But it’s going to be bad when you want something. You really have to go... You just can’t be running around on the road, or in town. You have to do something, to go to a doctor. Me, I’m going to have [medical help from family]—one’s going to be a doctor and two nursing. I’m proud that they’re doing that. One of my grandsons has finished [study at] Northeastern [university]. He’s working at Hastings. He’s 21 now. He wants to be an x-ray tech—that’s good. Well, you’re a doctor—it’s the same. If you want to be an x-ray tech, you have to go to school. And when you’re working inside the building, it’s warm. And you’re not working outside in the winter. He’s working at Hastings and he’s going to school, too, on some kind of program. He goes to school for four hours at Northeastern, and then he works 2-3 hours at night at Hastings. He’s hardly, he was telling me, he wasn’t making a lot of money. [I said] “But they’re still helping you, you’re going to school, and you have to buy gas. And something to eat—they pay for that.” He said, “Yeah, that’s true.” [I told him] “You can do what you want to do when you get done. You’ll be doing good.” He’s driving a pickup but really, it’s old. He’s had it since he was going to school. I told him, “I would help you if the automobile breaks down while you’re in school. But if you quit, I’m not going to help you. I’ll help you while you’re in school.” I told the other boy the same thing, “I’ll help you while you’re in school but if you quit, I’m not going to help you.” He’s a doctor now. It made me feel good, and two of them are nurses, and the other one—x-ray tech. It’d be good, if he don’t quit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As we’re finishing up, this is what I would like to say—if you think, I will give you the opportunity to say whatever you want to say.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: I don’t understand what you’re saying.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We’re finishing up now.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: If you think, “This is what I want—I want to say.” I’ll give you the opportunity to say. You can say whatever you want to say, and if you don’t, you can just tell me we’re done.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: We’re done.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are we done?

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: A’right. Thank you.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Me, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My name is Wa-le-li, in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-dewy-keener
segments.translation: Really? They call me Du-gi-na.
